items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The value of exports minus the value of imports"?
options: wealth effect
net exports (X − M)
sticky wages
deflationary (recessionary) gap
items.answer: net exports (X − M)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of net exports (X − M).

items.stem: Explain why the AD curve slopes downwards from left to right.
items.answer: A lower price level raises the real value of wealth (wealth effect), lowers interest rates as less money is needed for transactions (interest-rate effect), and makes exports more competitive (trade effect), so real spending rises.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A lower price level raises the real value of wealth (wealth effect), lowers interest rates as less money is needed for transactions (interest-rate effect), and makes exports more competitive (trade effect), so real spending rises. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that the AD curve slopes down because consumers buy more of a good when its price falls. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: That is the substitution effect for a single good; AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and international trade effects when the overall price level changes.
items.markingKey: That is the substitution effect for a single good; AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and international trade effects when the overall price level changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A briefing on Pacifica reports: household spending rose by $15 bn; business investment rose by $12 bn; public spending rose by $15 bn; export sales fell by $10 bn; spending on imports rose by $8 bn. Calculate the change in aggregate demand and state the direction in which the AD curve shifts.
items.answer: ΔAD = 15 + 12 + 15 + -10 − (8) = $24 bn; AD shifts to the right.
items.markingKey: ΔAD = ΔC + ΔI + ΔG + ΔX − ΔM = 24. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for $24 bn. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [A1] direction of shift.

items.stem: "The AD curve slopes down because consumers buy more of a good when its price falls." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That is the substitution effect for a single good; AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and international trade effects when the overall price level changes.
items.markingKey: That is the substitution effect for a single good; AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and international trade effects when the overall price level changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain, with the help of a fully labelled diagram, why the AD curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: Price level against real GDP; downward-sloping AD explained by the wealth effect, interest-rate effect and international trade effect (not the substitution effect for a single good).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Price level against real GDP; downward-sloping AD explained by the wealth effect, interest-rate effect and international trade effect (not the substitution effect for a single good). Level 3 (6-8) mostly accurate with some development. Level 2 (3-5) limited explanation or diagram errors. Level 1 (1-2) little understanding.

items.stem: Using the components of aggregate demand, explain how a 2-percentage-point rise in interest rates could affect AD in an economy where most mortgages have variable rates.
items.answer: Higher mortgage payments reduce disposable income and C; borrowing for durables falls; firms' cost of borrowing rises so I falls; higher rates may attract hot money, appreciating the currency and reducing X − M; AD shifts left. Effect larger with variable-rate mortgages.
items.markingKey: Higher mortgage payments reduce disposable income and C; borrowing for durables falls; firms' cost of borrowing rises so I falls; higher rates may attract hot money, appreciating the currency and reducing X − M; AD shifts left. Effect larger with variable-rate mortgages.

items.stem: "Consumer confidence is the most important determinant of aggregate demand." Discuss.
items.answer: Confidence is important because C is large, but the most important determinant depends on the economy and the shock; in small open economies foreign demand often dominates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: C is the largest component of AD; confidence changes amplify cycles through saving; confidence also affects investment. Arguments against: investment is more volatile and drives cycles; in open economies exports matter more (e.g. Germany, Ireland); confidence often follows rather than causes changes in income; interest rates and fiscal policy shape spending. Supported judgement: Confidence is important because C is large, but the most important determinant depends on the economy and the shock; in small open economies foreign demand often dominates. Markbands: IB Paper 1(b)/2(c) markbands [15]: Level 5 (13-15) relevant terms defined; theory explained clearly with an accurate, fully explained diagram where relevant; appropriate real-world examples; effective synthesis and a supported evaluation (short- vs long-run, stakeholders, assumptions, priorities). Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a fall in house prices can reduce aggregate demand.
items.answer: Households feel poorer (negative wealth effect) and have less collateral for borrowing, so they cut consumption; residential investment also falls.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Households feel poorer (negative wealth effect) and have less collateral for borrowing, so they cut consumption; residential investment also falls. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Higher imports increase aggregate demand because people are spending more." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Imports are spending on foreign output, so they are subtracted: higher M reduces AD for domestic output.
items.markingKey: Imports are spending on foreign output, so they are subtracted: higher M reduces AD for domestic output. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sticky wages"?
options: The point where AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect, so output equals potential output
The total quantity of real output firms plan to produce at each price level in the short run, when wages and other resource prices are fixed
The change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change
Money wages that do not adjust quickly to changes in the price level because of contracts and other factors
items.answer: Money wages that do not adjust quickly to changes in the price level because of contracts and other factors
items.markingKey: D. "sticky wages" is money wages that do not adjust quickly to changes in the price level because of contracts and other factors.

items.stem: A student claims that a fall in AD shifts the SRAS curve to the left. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A fall in AD moves the economy along the SRAS curve to lower output and price level; SRAS shifts only when costs of production change.
items.markingKey: A fall in AD moves the economy along the SRAS curve to lower output and price level; SRAS shifts only when costs of production change. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars writes: "A fall in AD shifts the SRAS curve to the left." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A fall in AD moves the economy along the SRAS curve to lower output and price level; SRAS shifts only when costs of production change.
items.markingKey: A fall in AD moves the economy along the SRAS curve to lower output and price level; SRAS shifts only when costs of production change. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A new subsidy for firms shifts AD to the right because firms have more money." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A production subsidy lowers firms' costs, so it shifts SRAS to the right (it may also affect AD indirectly).
items.markingKey: A production subsidy lowers firms' costs, so it shifts SRAS to the right (it may also affect AD indirectly). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the effect of a sharp rise in oil prices on short-run aggregate supply.
items.answer: AD/AS diagram: SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2; price level rises and real GDP falls (stagflation); explain higher costs of production.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: AD/AS diagram: SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2; price level rises and real GDP falls (stagflation); explain higher costs of production. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Supply shocks are a more serious problem for policymakers than demand shocks."
items.answer: Negative supply shocks are harder to manage because they create stagflation, but their seriousness depends on duration and on whether inflation expectations stay anchored.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: create a trade-off: rising inflation and falling output; demand-side policy cannot fix both; may raise inflation expectations. Arguments against: demand shocks can cause deep recessions (2008); supply shocks are often temporary; credible central banks can look through temporary price rises. Supported judgement: Negative supply shocks are harder to manage because they create stagflation, but their seriousness depends on duration and on whether inflation expectations stay anchored.

items.stem: Why does the SRAS curve slope upwards?
options: In the short run output prices rise while wages and other costs are fixed, so profits and production rise
Firms always operate at full capacity
Higher prices reduce costs
Consumers buy more at higher prices
items.answer: In the short run output prices rise while wages and other costs are fixed, so profits and production rise
items.markingKey: A. With sticky resource prices, higher output prices raise profitability.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that supply shocks are a more serious problem for policymakers than demand shocks.
items.answer: Negative supply shocks are harder to manage because they create stagflation, but their seriousness depends on duration and on whether inflation expectations stay anchored.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: create a trade-off: rising inflation and falling output; demand-side policy cannot fix both; may raise inflation expectations. Arguments against: demand shocks can cause deep recessions (2008); supply shocks are often temporary; credible central banks can look through temporary price rises. Supported judgement: Negative supply shocks are harder to manage because they create stagflation, but their seriousness depends on duration and on whether inflation expectations stay anchored.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "full employment level of output".
items.answer: The real GDP produced when unemployment is at its natural rate
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the real GDP produced when unemployment is at its natural rate. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the monetarist LRAS curve is vertical.
items.answer: In the long run wages and prices are flexible, so any change in the price level is matched by changes in costs; output is determined by the quantity and quality of resources and technology, not the price level.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the long run wages and prices are flexible, so any change in the price level is matched by changes in costs; output is determined by the quantity and quality of resources and technology, not the price level. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the Keynesian view of AS and the monetarist/new classical view of LRAS.
items.answer: Monetarists see LRAS as vertical at potential output because wages and prices are flexible, so the economy self-corrects; Keynesians see a horizontal section where output can stay below full employment because wages are sticky, so demand management is needed.
items.markingKey: Monetarists see LRAS as vertical at potential output because wages and prices are flexible, so the economy self-corrects; Keynesians see a horizontal section where output can stay below full employment because wages are sticky, so demand management is needed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that in the Keynesian model, an increase in AD always causes inflation. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level.
items.markingKey: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the US recovery after the 2008 crisis and explain what it reveals about spare capacity in the Keynesian model.
items.answer: After 2009 US unemployment took until 2016 to return to about 5%, and core inflation stayed below 2% for most of the period. Output could expand for years without inflationary pressure, consistent with a flat section of the AS curve
items.markingKey: Context (After 2009 US unemployment took until 2016 to return to about 5%, and core inflation stayed below 2% for most of the period.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Output could expand for years without inflationary pressure, consistent with a flat section of the AS curve – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to spare capacity in the Keynesian model.

items.stem: "In the Keynesian model, an increase in AD always causes inflation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level.
items.markingKey: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that economies will always return to full employment without government intervention.
items.answer: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wages and prices adjust over time; falling prices raise real wealth and AD; intervention may cause crowding out and inflation. Arguments against: wages are sticky downwards, so adjustment can take years; hysteresis: long-term unemployment reduces potential output; deflation can reduce AD further (debt-deflation); the 1930s and 2010s show slow recoveries. Supported judgement: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions.

items.stem: You are a policy adviser to the ministry of finance. A minister argues that economies will always return to full employment without government intervention. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: wages and prices adjust over time; falling prices raise real wealth and AD; intervention may cause crowding out and inflation. Counter-points: wages are sticky downwards, so adjustment can take years; hysteresis: long-term unemployment reduces potential output; deflation can reduce AD further (debt-deflation); the 1930s and 2010s show slow recoveries. Recommendation: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions. items.stem: Explain why the Keynesian AS curve has a horizontal section.
items.answer: With high unemployment and spare capacity, firms can expand output by using idle labour and capital without bidding up wages or input prices.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With high unemployment and spare capacity, firms can expand output by using idle labour and capital without bidding up wages or input prices. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the Great Depression of the 1930s and explain what it reveals about the Keynesian view of aggregate supply.
items.answer: US unemployment reached about 25% in 1933 and stayed above 14% for most of the decade. The economy did not quickly self-correct; prices fell but output stayed far below full employment, which supported Keynes's case for government spending
items.markingKey: Context (US unemployment reached about 25% in 1933 and stayed above 14% for most of the decade.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The economy did not quickly self-correct; prices fell but output stayed far below full employment, which supported Keynes's case for government spending – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the Keynesian view of aggregate supply.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stagflation"?
options: The point where AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect, so output equals potential output
Money wages that do not adjust quickly to changes in the price level because of contracts and other factors
The combination of rising inflation and falling (or stagnant) real output with rising unemployment
The ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in an injection (I, G or X): k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(MPS + MPT + MPM)
items.answer: The combination of rising inflation and falling (or stagnant) real output with rising unemployment
items.markingKey: C. "stagflation" is the combination of rising inflation and falling (or stagnant) real output with rising unemployment.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an inflationary gap in the monetarist model eventually closes through higher prices rather than more output.
items.answer: Above potential, labour is scarce, so wages rise; higher costs shift SRAS left until output returns to potential at a higher price level.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Above potential, labour is scarce, so wages rise; higher costs shift SRAS left until output returns to potential at a higher price level. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "In long-run equilibrium unemployment is zero." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Unemployment is at the natural rate (frictional + structural), which is positive.
items.markingKey: Unemployment is at the natural rate (frictional + structural), which is positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "An increase in AD always closes a deflationary gap without any inflation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: In the monetarist and in the upward-sloping section of the Keynesian model, higher AD also raises the price level.
items.markingKey: In the monetarist and in the upward-sloping section of the Keynesian model, higher AD also raises the price level. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline an inflationary gap in the Keynesian model.
items.answer: AD intersects the vertical section of the Keynesian AS curve; further increases in AD raise only the price level; the gap is the excess of AD over the level needed for full employment output.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: AD intersects the vertical section of the Keynesian AS curve; further increases in AD raise only the price level; the gap is the excess of AD over the level needed for full employment output. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Using an appropriate diagram, explain long-run equilibrium in the monetarist model.
items.answer: AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect at potential output Yp and price level P; no output gap; unemployment at the natural rate.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect at potential output Yp and price level P; no output gap; unemployment at the natural rate. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Closing a deflationary gap is best left to market forces."
items.answer: In shallow gaps market forces may suffice; deep and persistent gaps justify active fiscal and monetary support.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids fiscal deficits and debt; avoids policy errors and lags; wage flexibility restores equilibrium. Arguments against: slow adjustment raises long-term unemployment; hysteresis lowers potential output; falling prices can deepen recession. Supported judgement: In shallow gaps market forces may suffice; deep and persistent gaps justify active fiscal and monetary support.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that closing a deflationary gap is best left to market forces?
items.answer: In shallow gaps market forces may suffice; deep and persistent gaps justify active fiscal and monetary support.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids fiscal deficits and debt; avoids policy errors and lags; wage flexibility restores equilibrium. Arguments against: slow adjustment raises long-term unemployment; hysteresis lowers potential output; falling prices can deepen recession. items.stem: Briefly explain why a negative supply shock can create stagflation.
items.answer: SRAS shifts left, so at the new equilibrium the price level is higher and real output is lower, meaning inflation and unemployment rise together.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: SRAS shifts left, so at the new equilibrium the price level is higher and real output is lower, meaning inflation and unemployment rise together. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the euro area in 2012-2014 and explain what it reveals about a deflationary gap.
items.answer: Euro-area unemployment peaked above 12% in 2013 and inflation fell below 1%. Weak AD after the sovereign debt crisis left output below potential, creating spare capacity and low inflation
items.markingKey: Context (Euro-area unemployment peaked above 12% in 2013 and inflation fell below 1%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Weak AD after the sovereign debt crisis left output below potential, creating spare capacity and low inflation – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a deflationary gap.

items.stem: If the sum of the marginal propensities to save, tax and import is 0.25, what is the effect on real GDP of a $10 bn increase in investment?
options: $10 bn
$75 bn
$40 bn
items.answer: $40 bn

items.stem: Alessia writes: "A high marginal propensity to save makes the multiplier larger because savings fund investment." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Saving is a leakage from the circular flow; a higher MPS reduces the multiplier (k = 1/MPW).
items.markingKey: Saving is a leakage from the circular flow; a higher MPS reduces the multiplier (k = 1/MPW). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the average propensity to consume and the marginal propensity to consume.
items.answer: The MPC is the share of an additional dollar of income consumed; the APC is total consumption divided by total income.
items.markingKey: The MPC is the share of an additional dollar of income consumed; the APC is total consumption divided by total income. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If the multiplier is 4, a $10 bn tax cut raises GDP by $40 bn, exactly the same as a $10 bn rise in government spending." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Part of a tax cut is saved or spent on imports in the first round, so its initial injection is smaller than $10 bn; the effect of the tax cut is smaller than that of an equal rise in G.
items.markingKey: Part of a tax cut is saved or spent on imports in the first round, so its initial injection is smaller than $10 bn; the effect of the tax cut is smaller than that of an equal rise in G. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Data for Zedland: MPS = 0.15, MPT = 0.2, MPM = 0.25. Calculate the multiplier and the change in real GDP if investment by a foreign mining company rises by $40 bn.
items.markingKey: k = 1/(MPS + MPT + MPM) = 1/0.6 = 1.67; ΔY = 1.67 × 40 = 66.67. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for $66.67 bn. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that a large multiplier means that fiscal policy is always an effective way to close a deflationary gap.
items.answer: A large multiplier strengthens the case for fiscal policy in a deep recession, but uncertainty, lags and debt constraints limit its reliability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large k means a small injection has a big effect; effective when there is spare capacity; effective when monetary policy is at the zero lower bound. Arguments against: multiplier is uncertain and hard to estimate; time lags in implementation; crowding out and debt concerns; open economies leak spending through imports. Supported judgement: A large multiplier strengthens the case for fiscal policy in a deep recession, but uncertainty, lags and debt constraints limit its reliability.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Keynesian multiplier".
items.answer: The ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in an injection (I, G or X): k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(MPS + MPT + MPM)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in an injection (I, G or X): k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(MPS + MPT + MPM). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "wealth effect"?
options: The value of exports minus the value of imports
The level of real output and price level where AD intersects SRAS
An unexpected event that changes the costs of production and shifts SRAS
The change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change
items.answer: The change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change
items.markingKey: D. "wealth effect" is the change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change.

items.stem: In the monetarist/new classical model, what happens in the long run after an increase in AD?
options: The price level falls
The price level rises but real output returns to potential output
Unemployment falls permanently
Real output rises permanently
items.answer: The price level rises but real output returns to potential output
items.markingKey: B. LRAS is vertical; wages adjust to the higher price level.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "long-run equilibrium"?
options: The fraction of additional income that is saved
The fraction of additional income that is spent on domestic consumption
The change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change
The point where AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect, so output equals potential output
items.answer: The point where AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect, so output equals potential output
items.markingKey: D. "long-run equilibrium" is the point where AD, SRAS and LRAS intersect, so output equals potential output.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a change in costs of production and a change in the price level.
items.answer: A change in the price level causes a movement along SRAS; a change in costs of production (wages, raw materials, taxes, subsidies) shifts the SRAS curve.
items.markingKey: A change in the price level causes a movement along SRAS; a change in costs of production (wages, raw materials, taxes, subsidies) shifts the SRAS curve. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the multiplier effect may be smaller in practice than the simple formula suggests.
items.answer: Crowding out, rising prices if the economy is near capacity, time lags, and rising leakages (e.g. higher saving in uncertain times) reduce the effect on real output.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Crowding out, rising prices if the economy is near capacity, time lags, and rising leakages (e.g. higher saving in uncertain times) reduce the effect on real output. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between consumption and investment.
items.answer: Consumption is household spending on goods and services for current use; investment is firms' spending on capital goods that add to productive capacity.
items.markingKey: Consumption is household spending on goods and services for current use; investment is firms' spending on capital goods that add to productive capacity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Monetarists believe that AD has no effect on the economy at all." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Monetarists accept AD affects output in the short run along SRAS; in the long run only the price level is affected.
items.markingKey: Monetarists accept AD affects output in the short run along SRAS; in the long run only the price level is affected. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between long-run equilibrium and short-run equilibrium.
items.answer: Short-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS at any output; long-run equilibrium also requires output to equal potential, so AD = SRAS = LRAS.
items.markingKey: Short-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS at any output; long-run equilibrium also requires output to equal potential, so AD = SRAS = LRAS. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a depreciation of the currency can shift SRAS to the left.
items.answer: Imported raw materials, components and energy become more expensive in domestic currency, raising firms' costs of production.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Imported raw materials, components and energy become more expensive in domestic currency, raising firms' costs of production. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the US American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and explain what it reveals about the multiplier.
items.answer: The $787 bn package of spending and tax cuts aimed to offset the fall in AD after the financial crisis; the Congressional Budget Office estimated multipliers between about 0.4 and 2.5 for different components. Spending on infrastructure and transfers to low-income households (high MPC) had larger estimated multipliers than tax cuts for high earners
items.markingKey: Context (The $787 bn package of spending and tax cuts aimed to offset the fall in AD after the financial crisis; the Congressional Budget Office estimated multipliers between about 0.4 and 2.5 for different components.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the Keynesian AS curve with its three sections.

items.stem: A student claims that in long-run equilibrium unemployment is zero. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Unemployment is at the natural rate (frictional + structural), which is positive.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "A new subsidy for firms shifts AD to the right because firms have more money." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A production subsidy lowers firms' costs, so it shifts SRAS to the right (it may also affect AD indirectly).
items.markingKey: A production subsidy lowers firms' costs, so it shifts SRAS to the right (it may also affect AD indirectly). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the Keynesian multiplier effect of an increase in government spending.

items.stem: With reference to Germany's export dependence, explain how it illustrates net exports as a component of AD.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that economies will always return to full employment without government intervention.
items.answer: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: wages and prices adjust over time; falling prices raise real wealth and AD; intervention may cause crowding out and inflation. Arguments against: wages are sticky downwards, so adjustment can take years; hysteresis: long-term unemployment reduces potential output; deflation can reduce AD further (debt-deflation); the 1930s and 2010s show slow recoveries. Supported judgement: Self-correction may occur in the long run, but the costs of waiting can be high, which justifies counter-cyclical policy in deep recessions.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that closing a deflationary gap is best left to market forces.
items.answer: In shallow gaps market forces may suffice; deep and persistent gaps justify active fiscal and monetary support.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids fiscal deficits and debt; avoids policy errors and lags; wage flexibility restores equilibrium. Arguments against: slow adjustment raises long-term unemployment; hysteresis lowers potential output; falling prices can deepen recession. Supported judgement: In shallow gaps market forces may suffice; deep and persistent gaps justify active fiscal and monetary support. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that supply shocks are a more serious problem for policymakers than demand shocks.
items.answer: Negative supply shocks are harder to manage because they create stagflation, but their seriousness depends on duration and on whether inflation expectations stay anchored.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: create a trade-off: rising inflation and falling output; demand-side policy cannot fix both; may raise inflation expectations. items.stem: You are an analyst at a regional development bank. A minister argues that a large multiplier means that fiscal policy is always an effective way to close a deflationary gap. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: A large multiplier strengthens the case for fiscal policy in a deep recession, but uncertainty, lags and debt constraints limit its reliability.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: large k means a small injection has a big effect; effective when there is spare capacity; effective when monetary policy is at the zero lower bound. Counter-points: multiplier is uncertain and hard to estimate; time lags in implementation; crowding out and debt concerns; open economies leak spending through imports. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "aggregate demand (AD)".
items.answer: The total planned spending on an economy's goods and services at each possible price level in a given period: C + I + G + (X − M)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the total planned spending on an economy's goods and services at each possible price level in a given period: C + I + G + (X − M). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Keynesian AS curve".
items.answer: An aggregate supply curve with a horizontal section at low output, an upward-sloping section and a vertical section at full-employment output

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "short-run equilibrium"?
options: The level of real output and price level where AD intersects SRAS
The situation where equilibrium real GDP is below potential output, leaving unemployed resources
The combination of rising inflation and falling (or stagnant) real output with rising unemployment
The change in consumption caused by a change in the real value of households' wealth, for example when the price level or asset prices change
items.answer: The level of real output and price level where AD intersects SRAS
items.markingKey: A. "short-run equilibrium" is the level of real output and price level where AD intersects SRAS.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a change in the price level and a change in costs of production.
items.answer: A change in the price level causes a movement along SRAS; a change in costs of production (wages, raw materials, taxes, subsidies) shifts the SRAS curve.
items.markingKey: A change in the price level causes a movement along SRAS; a change in costs of production (wages, raw materials, taxes, subsidies) shifts the SRAS curve. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the multiplier process eventually stops.
items.answer: At each round a fraction of income leaks out of the circular flow as saving, taxes and imports, so successive rounds of spending become smaller until the total converges.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At each round a fraction of income leaks out of the circular flow as saving, taxes and imports, so successive rounds of spending become smaller until the total converges. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between consumption and investment.
items.answer: Consumption is household spending on goods and services for current use; investment is firms' spending on capital goods that add to productive capacity.
items.markingKey: Consumption is household spending on goods and services for current use; investment is firms' spending on capital goods that add to productive capacity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Keynesian view of AS and the monetarist/new classical view of LRAS.
items.answer: Monetarists see LRAS as vertical at potential output because wages and prices are flexible, so the economy self-corrects; Keynesians see a horizontal section where output can stay below full employment because wages are sticky, so demand management is needed.
items.markingKey: Monetarists see LRAS as vertical at potential output because wages and prices are flexible, so the economy self-corrects; Keynesians see a horizontal section where output can stay below full employment because wages are sticky, so demand management is needed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between short-run equilibrium and long-run equilibrium.
items.answer: Short-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS at any output; long-run equilibrium also requires output to equal potential, so AD = SRAS = LRAS.
items.markingKey: Short-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS at any output; long-run equilibrium also requires output to equal potential, so AD = SRAS = LRAS. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).
